node-1.label: Patient had decreased visual acuity in the right eye (20/80)

node-2.label: Patient had a history of strabismus, hyperopia, and amblyopia in the right eye, multiple odontogenic cysts, and scoliosis; she had been evaluated in Neuropediatrics for macrocephaly, her intellectual capacity was normal, and her mother had undergone surgery for skin cancer and maxillary cysts.

node-3.label: Clinical examination showed visual acuity of 20/80 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye; anterior segment evaluation showed no abnormalities, and intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes.

node-4.label: Fundus examination revealed an elevated white-greyish lesion in the temporal region of the macula with associated vascular distortion, causing significant traction in the macular area.

attrs.why: Radiologist analysis confirms that the decreased right-eye acuity (20/80), the elevated white-greyish macular lesion with vascular distortion, and the OCT/FA tractional findings together make a macular tractional lesion the most credible diagnosis, with all available key imaging already covered. This expert reaffirmation slightly raises confidence from 0.8 to 0.82.

Radiologist analysis notes the hyperreflective mass on OCT and FA leakage keep intraocular tumor/hamartoma in the differential, but it lacks B-scan confirmation and systemic imaging/genetic testing are incomplete. The same mass/leakage findings support it but do not confirm it, so confidence remains 0.6.

New OCT and FA evidence demonstrates organic macular pathology (disorganized retinal layers, hyperreflective mass, epiretinal membrane, vascular leakage). The radiologist supports macular traction as primary cause, further refuting amblyopia/refractive error as the sole explanation. Confidence decreases from 0.2 to 0.1.

Radiologist analysis notes that odontogenic cysts, macrocephaly, scoliosis, and family history of skin cancer/maxillary cysts suggest a systemic genetic syndrome, but genetic testing and brain MRI were not obtained and there is no direct link to the eye lesion. Confidence remains 0.4.

node-9.label: OCT shows disorganized retinal layers, hyperreflective mass, and epiretinal membrane

node-10.label: FA shows vascular tortuosity and leakage

node-11.label: Radiologist concluded that objective OCT/FA evidence supports macular tractional lesion as the most credible diagnosis

node-12.label: B-scan and systemic examinations are missing, and no genetic testing or brain MRI were obtained

node-13.label: Radiologist recommends clinical follow-up and consideration of vitrectomy evaluation

attrs.why: The radiologist explicitly favors epiretinal membrane-induced right macular traction as the leading diagnosis; OCT directly documents an epiretinal membrane with disorganized retinal layers and a hyperreflective mass, and FA shows tortuosity/leakage consistent with the observed vascular distortion. With this expert support the specific epiretinal-membrane mechanism becomes more likely, raising confidence from 0.8 to 0.85.

The radiologist's preference for an epiretinal membrane-based tractional mechanism, together with the absence of any explicit vitreous attachment to the macula on the available OCT, lowers the likelihood of vitreomacular traction syndrome. Confidence reduced from 0.4 to 0.28.

Current frontier is 'Macular tractional lesion'. An elevated white-greyish macular lesion with vascular distortion (node-4) could represent a tractional retinal detachment. However, no explicit detachment is noted on OCT or FA (node-9, node-10), so this is a less likely refinement.

node-17.label: Macular traction secondary to intraocular tumor/hamartoma

attrs.why: Current frontier is 'Macular tractional lesion'. The hyperreflective mass on OCT and FA leakage (node-9, node-10) could indicate an underlying tumor or hamartoma causing traction, as noted in the differential (node-6, score 0.6). This candidate refines the frontier by linking the traction to a specific mass-like etiology, though current consensus favors primary tractional lesion over tumor.

node-18.label: Available OCT/FA imaging describes no explicit vitreous attachment to the macula and no retinal detachment

node-19.label: Combined hamartoma of the retina and retinal pigment epithelium

attrs.why: The elevated white-greyish macular lesion with vascular distortion, together with the epiretinal membrane and hyperreflective mass on OCT, matches the morphology of a combined hamartoma of the retina and retinal pigment epithelium, a benign mass-like lesion that produces traction and vascular tortuosity in young patients. However, no B-scan or histology confirms it and the radiologist favors a primary epiretinal membrane, so confidence is moderate (0.35).

node-20.label: Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome)

attrs.why: Multiple odontogenic cysts, macrocephaly, scoliosis, and a maternal history of skin cancer and maxillary cysts closely match nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome), which features odontogenic keratocysts, macrocephaly, scoliosis, and basal cell carcinomas. attrs.why: The elevated white-greyish macular lesion with vascular distortion, together with the epiretinal membrane and hyperreflective mass on OCT, matches the morphology of a combined hamartoma of the retina and retinal pigment epithelium, a benign mass-like lesion that produces traction and vascular tortuosity in young patients. However, no B-scan or histology confirms it and the radiologist favors a primary epiretinal membrane, so confidence is moderate (0.35).

node-20.label: Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome)

attrs.why: Multiple odontogenic cysts, macrocephaly, scoliosis, and a maternal history of skin cancer and maxillary cysts closely match nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome), which features odontogenic keratocysts, macrocephaly, scoliosis, and basal cell carcinomas. Genetic testing and brain MRI are not yet available and no direct link to the eye lesion is established, so confidence is moderate (0.4).

node-1.label: Patient had decreased visual acuity in the right eye (20/80)

node-2.label: Patient had a history of strabismus, hyperopia, and amblyopia in the right eye, multiple odontogenic cysts, and scoliosis; she had been evaluated in Neuropediatrics for macrocephaly, her intellectual capacity was normal, and her mother had undergone surgery for skin cancer and maxillary cysts.

node-3.label: Clinical examination showed visual acuity of 20/80 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye; anterior segment evaluation showed no abnormalities, and intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes.

node-4.label: Fundus examination revealed an elevated white-greyish lesion in the temporal region of the macula with associated vascular distortion, causing significant traction in the macular area.

attrs.why: Radiologist analysis confirms that the decreased right-eye acuity (20/80), the elevated white-greyish macular lesion with vascular distortion, and the OCT/FA tractional findings together make a macular tractional lesion the most credible diagnosis, with all available key imaging already covered. This expert reaffirmation slightly raises confidence from 0.8 to 0.82.

Radiologist analysis notes the hyperreflective mass on OCT and FA leakage keep intraocular tumor/hamartoma in the differential, but it lacks B-scan confirmation and systemic imaging/genetic testing are incomplete. The same mass/leakage findings support it but do not confirm it, so confidence remains 0.6.

New OCT and FA evidence demonstrates organic macular pathology (disorganized retinal layers, hyperreflective mass, epiretinal membrane, vascular leakage). The radiologist supports macular traction as primary cause, further refuting amblyopia/refractive error as the sole explanation. Confidence decreases from 0.2 to 0.1.

Radiologist analysis notes that odontogenic cysts, macrocephaly, scoliosis, and family history of skin cancer/maxillary cysts suggest a systemic genetic syndrome, but genetic testing and brain MRI were not obtained and there is no direct link to the eye lesion. Confidence remains 0.4.

node-10.label: FA shows vascular tortuosity and leakage

node-11.label: Radiologist concluded that objective OCT/FA evidence supports macular tractional lesion as the most credible diagnosis

attrs.why: The radiologist explicitly favors epiretinal membrane-induced right macular traction as the leading diagnosis; OCT directly documents an epiretinal membrane with disorganized retinal layers and a hyperreflective mass, and FA shows tortuosity/leakage consistent with the observed vascular distortion. With this expert support the specific epiretinal-membrane mechanism becomes more likely, raising confidence from 0.8 to 0.85.

The radiologist's preference for an epiretinal membrane-based tractional mechanism, together with the absence of any explicit vitreous attachment to the macula on the available OCT, lowers the likelihood of vitreomacular traction syndrome. Confidence reduced from 0.4 to 0.28.

Current frontier is 'Macular tractional lesion'. An elevated white-greyish macular lesion with vascular distortion (node-4) could represent a tractional retinal detachment. However, no explicit detachment is noted on OCT or FA (node-9, node-10), so this is a less likely refinement.

node-17.label: Macular traction secondary to intraocular tumor/hamartoma

attrs.why: Current frontier is 'Macular tractional lesion'. The hyperreflective mass on OCT and FA leakage (node-9, node-10) could indicate an underlying tumor or hamartoma causing traction, as noted in the differential (node-6, score 0.6). This candidate refines the frontier by linking the traction to a specific mass-like etiology, though current consensus favors primary tractional lesion over tumor.
